extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants (U.S. §101 subject-matter eligibility analysis)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and worked examples for analyzing patent claims under the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (2019 PEG), focusing on identifying judicial exceptions and determining whether claims are integrated into a practical application or provide an inventive concept. Intended to be used when examining or drafting claims for Section 101 compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Category (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a series of steps it may be a process; identify the statutory category as the first step in the eligibility analysis. (Examples: claims in the examples are analyzed as processes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Prong 1: Judicial Exception Recited?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception (abstract idea), such as a mathematical concept/formula, a mental process, or a certain method of organizing human activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a judicial exception, proceed to Prong 2 to determine whether the exception is integrated into a practical application. Examples show identifying mental processes (e.g., calculating amount of use), mathematical formulas (e.g., modular arithmetic in cryptography), and methods of organizing human activity (e.g., managing interactions between people/medical record notifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental Processes Group
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation is a 'mental process' if, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, it covers performance in the human mind (or using pen and paper) rather than requiring something beyond mental performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the limitation could practically be performed in the mind except for a nominal recitation of a generic computer/processor. Mere insertion of 'by a processor' does not remove a step from the mental-process grouping (Example 37, 39, 40 analyses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that explicitly recite a mathematical relationship, formula, or calculation are judicial exceptions (mathematical concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a mathematical formula is recited, evaluate whether the combination of additional elements uses the mathematical concepts in a specific manner that limits their use to a practical application (Example 41: modular arithmetic in cryptography integrated into securing network communications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of Organizing Human Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are methods of organizing human activity (e.g., fundamental economic concepts, managing interactions between people) are judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include methods that manage how people interact or share information (Example 42: transmission of notifications when medical records are updated is a method of managing interactions between people). If so, proceed to determine whether additional elements integrate the idea into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Prong 2: Integration into a Practical Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the additional claim elements, individually and in combination, integrate the judicial exception into a practical application such that the claim is not directed to the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the claim as a whole provides a specific improvement (e.g., improved user interface, improved network monitoring) or otherwise applies the exception in a particularized way. If the additional elements amount to more than nominal/generic recitations and provide a specific technological improvement, the claim may be 'not directed to' the judicial exception (Examples 37, 40, 41, 42 analyses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific Technical/Technological Improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a specific improvement to computer functionality or other technology (e.g., improved user interface, reduced network traffic, improved audio simulation fidelity) supports integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify factual assertions of a specific improvement over prior systems (Example 37: improved GUI by automatically displaying most-used icons closer to start icon; Example 40: limiting NetFlow data collection to abnormal conditions reduces network burden; Example 38: simulating analog variances for improved audio quality). Such statements support finding the claim integrates the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic Computer Components Are Insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere nominal recitation of generic computer components (e.g., 'a processor', 'a network appliance', 'a content server') does not integrate an abstract idea into a practical application or provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements are recited at a high level of generality and merely automate the abstract idea, they are 'no more than mere instructions to apply the exception using a generic computer component' (Examples 37, 39, 40, 42 show this anti-pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity / Data Gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed steps that amount to mere data gathering, receiving signals, or other pre-/post-solution activity are treated as insignificant extra-solution activity and generally do not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting or receiving data in a generic manner (e.g., collecting network statistics, receiving a plaintext signal) is often considered insignificant; such limitations should be re-examined at Step 2B to determine if they are well-understood, routine, and conventional (Examples 40, 41, 42).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Inventive Concept (Significantly More)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether claim additional elements, individually or in combination, provide an 'inventive concept' — i.e., something significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether any additional elements impose meaningful limits beyond the exception and are not merely conventional or routine. If they do provide significantly more, the claim may be eligible; otherwise, it is ineligible (Examples: claims found ineligible where additional elements were generic or conventional; Example 41 shows mathematical concept integrated into application and found eligibility at 2A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional Inquiry (2B Re-evaluation / Berkheimer Considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Step 2B, decide whether claimed additional elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional activity; if so, they do not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background and evidence of conventionality matters. The guidance notes that an element considered insignificant extra-solution activity in 2A should be re-evaluated in 2B to determine conventionality (Example 40's collecting step determined to be well-understood, routine, conventional). Case law (e.g., Berkheimer) is invoked for this re-evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration vs. Inventive Concept Distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A Prong 2 examines integration of an exception into a practical application (i.e., whether claim as a whole is directed to the exception), while Step 2B examines whether additional elements supply an inventive concept (i.e., 'significantly more').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an exception is integrated into a practical application at Step 2A (making the claim 'not directed to' an exception), Step 2B is not always applicable. Conversely, if Step 2A finds the claim directed to an exception, Step 2B asks whether the claim's additional elements supply significantly more (see Example 41 discussion and notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit Recitation of Mathematical Formula vs. Use of Mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim explicitly reciting a mathematical formula or calculation is treated as reciting a mathematical concept; however, use of math in service of a specific technological application can integrate the concept into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the mathematical formula is explicitly claimed (e.g., modular exponentiation in cryptographic encoding), analyze whether the claim applies the mathematics in a specific manner that secures communications or achieves a specific technological result (Example 41: cryptography math integrated into securing communication was treated as integrated and eligible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation of Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: All claims are analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining whether a limitation is a mental process or otherwise an exception, analyze the claim under its broadest reasonable interpretation; hypothetical variations of performance (e.g., manual vs. computer-performed) can affect whether a limitation falls into a judicial exception (Examples 37 and 39 discuss how 'by a processor' may not remove mental-process characterization under broad interpretation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Must Also Meet Other Patentability Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter eligibility (Section 101) is only one requirement; all claims must ultimately be analyzed for compliance with every requirement for patentability, including 35 U.S.C. §§ 102, 103, and 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PEG examples explicitly note that the §101 analysis does not address novelty, non-obviousness, or written description/enablement, which must be considered separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples Are Illustrative and Fact-Specific
rubrics_metrics.description: The examples are hypothetical, illustrative of claim analysis under the 2019 PEG, and should be interpreted based on the specific fact patterns set forth; different fact patterns may lead to different eligibility outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary for a claim to mirror an example to be eligible; use the examples only as guidance and consider case-specific facts and claim wording.
